strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: training-free reward alignment of pretrained discrete diffusion models while retaining an explicit KL-regularized target distribution.

Combining twisted SMC with a tractable, reward-aware proposal is intuitive, and the treatment of masked-model discontinuities through a continuous formulation and Gumbel-Softmax is practically motivated.
The synthetic experiment usefully compares the approximate proposal with an exact locally optimal proposal and reports reward, Earth Mover's Distance, diversity, and ESS trajectories.
The appendix provides substantial derivational detail, connects the discrete-time construction to continuous-time SMC, and reports key sampling hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evaluation is far below top-tier standards. It is limited to two-dimensional toy mixtures and binarized MNIST with a single target class and alpha value. MNIST evidence consists mainly of small qualitative grids and classifier reward, with no distributional quality metrics, class-conditional accuracy from an independent evaluator, uncertainty estimates, or repeated trials.

The baseline set is exceptionally narrow: the only guidance baseline is essentially the same first-order approximation without tempering or resampling. Relevant discrete guidance, derivative-free control, SMC guidance, and alignment or fine-tuning methods discussed in the related-work section are not evaluated.

The claim that the proposal in Eq. 11 constitutes an 'optimal twisting function' and enables exact target samples with a single particle is not adequately justified and appears generally incorrect. A globally optimal twist normally involves a backward information function such as a conditional expectation of the terminal potential; exp(lambda_t E[r(X)|z_t]/alpha) is not generally equal to E[exp(r(X)/alpha)|z_t]. Local minimization of incremental-weight variance does not by itself imply exact terminal sampling with one particle.

The claimed asymptotic unbiasedness is insufficiently supported when the intermediate reward is approximated using fresh Monte Carlo samples and Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. The paper does not formalize the randomness as an extended-state SMC construction or establish that the implemented weight calculations still target the stated terminal distribution.

The proposed method is expensive—requiring particles, denoiser and reward gradients at every step, reward Monte Carlo estimates, and resampling—but there is no runtime, memory, particle-count scaling, or quality-versus-compute comparison. The toy setting even uses 2,000 particles.

Novelty is modest relative to prior SMC alignment and existing first-order Taylor guidance for discrete diffusion. The empirical study does not isolate the contributions of Taylor approximation, Gumbel-Softmax, tempering, partial resampling, or the special continuous carry-over formulation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: denoiser and classifier training details, Gumbel-Softmax temperature and estimator choices, random seeds, dataset/model performance, tuning protocol, and code availability are absent. The admitted hand-tuning of schedules and thresholds further raises concerns about robustness and generalization.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: training-free reward alignment of pretrained discrete diffusion models.
Combining twisted SMC with a gradient-based approximation to the locally optimal proposal is technically plausible and potentially useful.

The derivation connects the proposal, importance weights, and masked-diffusion parameterization reasonably clearly; the appendix also discusses extensions to ReMDM, uniform-noise diffusion, and continuous-time formulations.

The synthetic experiment includes an oracle locally optimal proposal and shows that the proposed approximation can reduce distributional error and weight degeneracy relative to using the reverse process alone.
The authors acknowledge important limitations, including sensitivity to the tempering schedule and the absence of evidence on realistic applications.
weaknesses: The evaluation is far too limited for a top-tier conference. It covers only two-dimensional synthetic mixtures and binarized MNIST, with the latter evaluated on a single target digit and a single alignment strength.

The MNIST evidence is almost entirely qualitative: only 20 displayed particles and their classifier reward are reported. There are no aggregate results over test samples, seeds, target classes, or alignment strengths, and no quantitative measures of fidelity, coverage, diversity, or target accuracy.

The baseline set is inadequate. The experiments omit the strongest and most relevant discrete-diffusion guidance and SMC methods discussed in the related-work section, including the closely related method of Lee et al. (2025). Comparing mainly against an intentionally approximate, untempered guidance baseline does not establish competitiveness.

The claimed practical advantage is not supported by computational measurements. The method requires multiple particles, repeated denoiser evaluations, reward estimation, backpropagation through the denoiser and reward, and sometimes 100 reward samples per particle per step, yet runtime, memory, and scaling are never reported.

The novelty appears incremental: SMC alignment, locally optimal proposals, Taylor approximations for discrete guidance, and Gumbel-Softmax differentiation are all established ingredients. The paper does not demonstrate that their combination yields a substantial advance on a realistic task.

The statement that the locally optimal proposal enables exact sampling from the target with a single particle is generally incorrect or, at minimum, seriously underqualified. A locally optimal proposal removes conditional variance in the current incremental weight, but the remaining normalizing factor can depend on the ancestor; one-particle SMC therefore does not generally produce an exact target sample.

The treatment of stochastic reward estimation and Gumbel-Softmax gradients is underspecified. The paper does not explain whether auxiliary randomness is included in the importance-sampling construction or prove that the resulting noisy proposals and potentials preserve the claimed asymptotic correctness.

Equation (18) presents the per-token proposal as an equality without the required normalization constants. Other consequential details—Gumbel temperature, gradient estimator variance, numerical stabilization, and exact handling of proposal probabilities—are missing.

The experiments admit substantial hand-tuning of the tempering schedule, ESS threshold, and other parameters to obtain good MNIST results, but provide no sensitivity analysis or principled selection procedure. This weakens both robustness and reproducibility.

Reproducibility is insufficient: model and classifier training details, architecture specifications, checkpoint quality, preprocessing, seed variability, EMD computation, and complete resampling implementation are not documented adequately.

Overall, the method is plausible and the toy evidence is encouraging, but the unsupported exactness language, weak empirical scope, missing competitive baselines, and lack of quantitative or efficiency evaluation prevent the submission from meeting the acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: training-free test-time alignment of discrete diffusion models while explicitly preserving proximity to the pretrained distribution.

The combination of twisted SMC, a reward-aware proposal, and a Gumbel-Softmax-based gradient construction is intuitive and potentially useful. The proposed proposal empirically improves reward, diversity, and distributional accuracy over using the unguided reverse process.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper provides useful derivations, an algorithm, discussion of several discrete diffusion parameterizations, and a connection to continuous-time SMC.
The synthetic experiments include an exact target and locally optimal oracle, enabling informative comparisons using reward, EMD, diversity, and ESS traces.
The MNIST results consistently illustrate the practical advantage of allowing remasking or token modification during guided generation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially below the standard for a top-tier conference. It is restricted to two-dimensional synthetic mixtures and binarized MNIST, with only one displayed target digit. There are no modern language, molecular, protein, graph, or other realistically high-dimensional discrete-generation experiments.

The empirical evidence is mostly qualitative and based on single runs. MNIST lacks aggregate success rates, sample-quality or diversity metrics, uncertainty estimates, results over all classes and reward strengths, particle-count scaling, runtime, memory, and comparisons at matched compute.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. The main comparison is a first-order approximate-guidance baseline closely related to the proposed proposal. The paper does not empirically compare against the broader discrete-guidance, SMC, inference-time scaling, or alignment methods discussed in its own related-work section.

The claim that the locally optimal proposal enables exact sampling from the target with a single particle is generally incorrect. The proposal minimizes conditional incremental-weight variance, but its normalizing constant can depend on the ancestor, so a one-particle trajectory does not in general have the desired marginal distribution.

The mathematical specification has important ambiguities. Equation 18 writes an equality using unnormalized categorical factors, while exact evaluation of the proposal probability is required by the SMC weights. The use of Monte Carlo reward estimates and fresh Gumbel samples inside intermediate potentials is not described carefully enough to establish the claimed asymptotic unbiasedness.

Novelty is limited because SMC for discrete diffusion and first-order Taylor approximations for discrete guidance already exist. The paper's contribution is mainly their combination plus a masked-model gradient construction, without sufficiently strong experiments to demonstrate broader significance.

Performance depends on a carefully hand-designed tempering schedule and other task-specific choices. There is no sensitivity analysis for these choices, despite the paper acknowledging that masked-diffusion results were difficult to obtain.

Reproducibility is incomplete: architectural and training details are sparse, the partial-resampling implementation is underspecified, and no code or sufficiently detailed protocol is provided. Overall, the idea is promising, but the unsupported theoretical statement and preliminary evaluation make the submission not yet competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem—controlling pretrained discrete diffusion models at inference time—and presents a conceptually appealing SMC framework with gradient-based and amortised proposal variants.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering controlled language generation, DNA design, ImageNet generation, text-to-image alignment, and controlled synthetic experiments.
Several results are promising: increasing the particle count often improves alignment or sample quality, and the amortised proposal generally outperforms the base-model proposal.
The appendix provides proofs, implementation details, hyperparameters, sampling comparisons, ablations, and extensive qualitative examples.
weaknesses: A central soundness claim is unjustified. Equation (7) uses the approximate detailed-balance identity between the learned reverse model and the prescribed forward process, yet the paper states that choosing the forward kernel eliminates this approximation error. For an imperfect learned reverse model, the identity generally does not hold, so the resulting SMC procedure is not established to target the claimed reward-tilted distribution or to be asymptotically unbiased.

Proposition 3 appears incorrect as stated. Under the claimed locally optimal proposal, the incremental log-weight equals log Z(x_t)-r(x_t), which generally depends on x_t. The auxiliary baseline F_psi(t) depends only on time and therefore cannot make the proposed squared loss zero in general. Consequently, the proof's assertion that the optimum is zero, and hence its uniqueness and recovery of the locally optimal proposal, does not follow.

The treatment of low-confidence sampling changes the pretrained transition by using the learned proposal's logits to choose which positions are updated. The paper does not prove that this proposal-dependent transition preserves the intended pretrained marginal or target distribution, further weakening the claimed correctness of importance weighting.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Strong contemporary alignment and SMC baselines are largely absent, compute-matched comparisons are not provided, and the benefits of up to 16 particles are reported without wall-clock cost, memory use, effective sample size, or comparisons against spending equivalent computation on best-of-N or additional denoising steps.

Evidence for the amortised objective's stated mechanism is limited: reward curves do not demonstrate reduced importance-weight variance, proximity to the optimal proposal, reduced particle degeneracy, or improved effective sample size.

The text-to-image experiments primarily evaluate with the same reward models used for optimisation, with no human evaluation or independent holdout metrics. One task uses only 45 curated animal prompts, and uncertainty or repeated-seed statistics are generally missing.

There are material reporting inconsistencies: for the same N=8 SMCamot language experiment, Table 1 reports 99.7% holdout toxicity, perplexity 147.6, and diversity 44/81/91, whereas Table 4 reports 100.0%, 127.0, and 43/81/91. Such discrepancies undermine confidence in the results.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive hyperparameter reporting: important proposal architecture, reference-distribution, resampling, checkpoint-selection, and evaluation details are insufficient, and no code or artifact release is identified.

The toxicity experiment deliberately optimises generation of harmful text. Although examples carry a warning, the paper lacks a substantive risk analysis, justification of the experimental design, or discussion of release safeguards.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: inference-time control and scaling of pretrained discrete diffusion models without requiring access to their original training data.
The proposed framework covers both product-distribution targets and reward tilting, and the discussion usefully emphasizes the often-overlooked effect of proposal quality on SMC performance.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, spanning controlled synthetic examples, language, regulatory DNA design, ImageNet generation, and text-to-image alignment.

Several experiments show substantial empirical gains as the particle count increases. The language evaluation includes a separate holdout toxicity classifier, and the DNA experiment reports multiple seeds and comparisons with established baselines.
The appendix provides derivations, implementation discussion for several masked-diffusion sampling schemes, hyperparameters, ablations, and qualitative samples.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification for the amortized proposal appears incorrect. Proposition 3 assumes that the loss in Equation (10) can reach zero at the locally optimal proposal, but its baseline F_psi depends only on time. At the optimal conditional proposal, the log incremental weight generally contains a normalizing term that depends on x_t, not only on t. Consequently, the stated zero-loss argument and uniqueness conclusion do not follow, and minimizing the proposed surrogate under an arbitrary reference distribution need not recover the locally optimal proposal.

The claim that SMC is an asymptotically unbiased sampler is overstated for the implemented setting. The target-density ratios are replaced using an approximate detailed-balance relation involving a learned reverse model. Unless that model is an exact reversal of the selected forward process, increasing the number of particles removes Monte Carlo error but not this model-induced bias. The reward estimates and low-confidence modification introduce further approximations.

The low-confidence construction in Equation (45) changes the base transition so that its token-selection decision uses the learned proposal's logits. It is not adequately established that the resulting weight corrects toward the originally claimed pretrained-model target. This is especially consequential because the large-scale text-to-image results use this construction.

Experimental comparisons do not isolate the contribution of SMC or establish compute efficiency. The amortized method receives substantial full-model or LoRA fine-tuning, yet it is usually compared with pretrained proposals, guidance, or best-of-N rather than compute-matched RL, direct-reward fine-tuning, GFlowNet, or recent SMC alignment methods. Only the DNA experiment includes a reasonably strong fine-tuning baseline.

The text-to-image evaluation relies exclusively on the same learned reward models used for optimization. It lacks held-out reward models, human judgments, standard image-quality/diversity measurements, and uncertainty estimates, leaving reward overfitting as a strong alternative explanation. Prompt-set sizes, evaluation sample counts, and variability are also incompletely reported.

Most reported results lack confidence intervals or repeated-seed statistics. Figure 5 has no uncertainty bars, the language results use only 300 samples without significance analysis, and synthetic results are largely qualitative. Several important design choices, including reward scaling, entropy or KL regularization, schedules, and sampling rules, vary by domain and are only sparsely ablated.

Novelty is limited by substantial prior work on SMC for inference-time steering of discrete diffusion models and by the fact that the gradient proposal resembles existing discrete guidance. The amortized log-variance objective is the main differentiator, but it is precisely the component whose theoretical characterization is unsupported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or artifact release is identified, and essential architectural details for the proposal and baseline network, LoRA configuration, reference-distribution construction, resampling implementation, and total compute comparisons are missing.

The toxicity experiment deliberately optimizes generation of harmful text. Although the paper includes a warning, it provides little ethical analysis, justification, or discussion of model-release and misuse safeguards.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable inference-time control of pretrained discrete diffusion models without requiring access to their original training data.
The proposed unifying SMC perspective is intuitive and potentially useful, and the emphasis on proposal design identifies a practically important source of particle degeneracy.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering controlled synthetic distributions, language generation, DNA design, ImageNet generation, and large-scale text-to-image generation.

Several results are compelling: increasing particle count substantially improves FID/IS in low-step ImageNet sampling, holdout toxicity scores support alignment beyond the training classifier, and the DNA study includes comparisons against established guidance and fine-tuning baselines.
The paper provides useful implementation details, hyperparameter ablations, sample-quality metrics, qualitative examples, and some multi-seed reporting.
weaknesses: A central theoretical claim appears incorrect. Proposition 3 concludes that the proposed loss uniquely recovers the locally optimal proposal by asserting that its minimum is zero. However, under the locally optimal proposal, the incremental log-weight generally retains an x_t-dependent normalizing constant, while the auxiliary F_psi depends only on t. Thus the loss need not attain zero, and minimizing this upper bound does not establish recovery of the locally optimal proposal. This undermines the main justification for the amortized method.

The claim that approximation error is eliminated for reward tilting is insufficiently justified. Cancelling the diffusion marginal ratio still relies on the learned reverse transition satisfying detailed balance with the prescribed forward process, which is generally only approximate for a pretrained denoiser. Consequently, descriptions of the method as asymptotically unbiased or exact for the intended tilted target are overstated.

The continuous-time derivation contains inconsistent notation about which rate matrix represents the forward, reverse, and proposal processes, making Proposition 1 difficult to verify. The appendix also contains direction and denominator inconsistencies in the proof of Proposition 2, even though its high-level result is standard.

The strongest text-to-image evidence primarily reports the same learned reward used for optimization. There is no independent human evaluation or held-out alignment metric, and comparisons against strong reward-alignment or fine-tuning baselines are missing. Reward improvement alone cannot rule out reward-model exploitation or quality/diversity degradation.

Compute-matched comparisons are incomplete. SMC variants use multiple particles and repeated reward evaluations, while SMC_amot additionally requires substantial fine-tuning; the paper does not report wall-clock cost, memory, reward-model calls, or comparisons at equal compute. This weakens the inference-time-scaling claim.

Reproducibility is limited by missing code and underspecified proposal architectures, reference-distribution choices, evaluation sample counts for several text-to-image experiments, and model-selection procedures. Some reported experiments also lack uncertainty estimates.

The language experiment is small (300 generations) and explicitly maximizes toxicity. Although a warning is included, the paper provides little ethical discussion of the dual-use risk or safeguards for releasing a general mechanism that strengthens harmful-output optimization.
